records.name: Liberia
records.summary: Liberia is dangerous for trans visitors. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never colonised); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no LGR.

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Oct 2024): Rep. Johnson N. Williams is seeking lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer; related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex — documents active legislative threat beyond the existing statute.

UNDP/OHCHR 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia Country Report' (April 2020): participatory review and analysis of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia.

NPR (9 Apr 2012, 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight'): anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The Guardian (19 Mar 2012, Monrovia): Nobel Peace Prize president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview; her remarks drew international comment on Liberia's stance (Blair declined to comment).

records.name: Djibouti
records.summary: Djibouti is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): penal code §§ 353–354 refer vaguely to 'good morals' with no explicit criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, yet their at-a-glance table still marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; current-fact: still no explicit offence, but 'obscene acts'/public morality provisions are used against people.

Wikipedia overview (current): legality of same-sex conduct is ambiguous — no law says either way, but authorities can prosecute public same-sex conduct under 'good morals' provisions, so it is treated as de facto illegal; discrimination protection exists in employment only; no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Djibouti SOGIESC section: law does not explicitly criminalise consensual LGBTQI+ conduct, but status and conduct are taboo; a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable — complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH); no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination; pervasive social and religious intolerance makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) - baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request DJI104070.E (research 2009–Mar 2012, via ecoi.net): documentation on treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti was scarce across all consulted sources, leaning on the US 2010 country report — a dated historical baseline showing how little legal/protection framework and support services existed in that period.

records.name: Guinea-Bissau
records.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal — one of few nations in the region never to criminalise it: a 1993 penal code decree omits same-sex offences and a 2014 domestic-violence law protects victims regardless of sexual orientation. No legal gender recognition, no trans framework and no partnership recognition exist, and there is no anti-discrimination protection, so no document or screening pathway for trans travelers is documented.

Enforcement and practical safety dominate: chronic instability (a 2012 coup), a weak national apparatus, documented impunity for security-force abuse (arbitrary killings, torture), documented social hostility and stigma, some violence cases in 2018, no visible LGBT scene, and a poor 34/100 ('Caution') travel-safety score, with no mob-lynching pattern reported for a neighbouring nation.

sources.summary: US State Dept 2012 report on Guinea-Bissau: documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity; notes no criminalisation of same-sex conduct — general security context for visitors.
US State Dept 2011 report: security-force torture, FGM and impunity documented; the LGBT section notes no criminalisation but societal stigma against LGBT people.

Overview of LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau: same-sex conduct legal since 1993 (penal code decree 4/93 omits same-sex offences); signed the 2008 UN SOGI statement; only married heterosexual couples entitled to larger government housing; domestic-violence law (6/2014) Article 5 protects victims regardless of sexual orientation.
LiquiSearch: LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau - brief overview page (Wikipedia-derived) noting legal challenges and sections on same-sex activity, relationships, adoption and living conditions.

Mapa.gay country guide for Guinea-Bissau: legal since 1993; no partnership recognition; no trans framework; travel-safety score 34/100 ('Caution'); 9% consider homosexual behaviour morally acceptable — unusually moderate for West Africa; no visible LGBT scene; some violence cases (2018).

records.name: Eswatini
records.summary: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 March 2026: same-sex relations ILLEGAL for men and women throughout Eswatini; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations NOT able to register.
Freedom in the World 2024: Eswatini rated Not Free with an overall score of 17/100 (Political Rights 1/40, Civil Liberties 16/60) - an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

BTI 2024 country report: the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations, within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment ('Mswati must fall' having become a common protest slogan).

US State Department 2021 report on Eswatini: some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June, LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident.
Swazi Media Commentary of December 2018: a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened - religious-space inclusion documented alongside 'no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom'.

MambaOnline, July 2018: the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect success' - the inaugural Pride in the kingdom, marking public LGBT visibility in a state where same-sex conduct remains illegal.
MambaOnline, July 2019: Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group - the documented administrative blocking of organisational recognition in the kingdom.
